probably not a good idea

to just use any old TVS
diode on an RF line.
I'm gonna explain why in this video,
let's hop in and get started.
(upbeat music)
So on a recent one minute design review
for Christoph Schmied, I pointed out
that it is not always best practice
to use a TVS diode on an RF line.

was for generation of harmonics.

Now, there were or some
questions about this,
and I've highlighted a few here on screen.
Here you can see from Pleo Maxple,
what if ESD protection is needed,
what would be the right approach?

Daniel Macrae also asks, wondering
the same thing as others,

how do we protect against
ESD on the antenna input

These are both really great questions
and you can use TVS diodes on RF lines
if they are selected properly
and they have certain characteristics.

Now, there are some
things to watch out for
when selecting the TVS diode

as well as you need to
understand the non-linear nature

of TVS diodes, so that you
don't generate new harmonics
or intermodulation products,
as I pointed out in the design review.
So let's hop on the board.

I'll guide you through selecting
TVS diodes for RF lines.
So to get a sense

for how to select TVS
diodes for an RF line,

let's take a look at the
situation in question.
So here we're considering a situation
where maybe we have an antenna

and that antenna connects
to a transmission line.
That transmission line
then connects to the RX pin on a receiver.

And then somewhere along
this transmission line
we have a TVS diode.
Now, the TVS diode could be unidirectional

and then connect to ground,
or it could be bidirectional.
So which one do we need?

Well, in this case, we're
just going to assume
that we have a simple AC wave

that is propagating on
the transmission line,
and of course, that AC wave

has positive and negative
voltage associated with it,

and then there is some
frequency associated with it.
So of course,

because it is oscillating
above and below zero volts,

we would want to have the
bidirectional TVS diode.

Now, if there was some
DC offset on this signal,

for example, maybe it's
oscillating up here like this,
then it would make sense to have

a unidirectional TVS
diode for this RF line.

But because typically, we're
dealing with this sign wave,
it oscillates above and below zero,
we want that bidirectional TVS diode.

So that's our first
requirement in general,
for a TVS diode on an RF line,
we want it to be bidirectional.

Now, if you're unsure of
how these components work

for unidirectional or
bidirectional TVS diodes,

check out the video
link in the description

it goes over these
components in more detail.

Now, when the wave encounters
the TVS diode along this line,
we have to look at the transfer function

or the transfer characteristic
of the TVS diode
in order to understand

how this component
interacts with this wave.
When we have a curve like this

showing the current versus
voltage applied on the TVS diode,

we generally have a forward
bias transfer function
that looks something like this.
Eventually we get to a forward voltage

and then it starts conducting
in the forward direction.

And since this is a
bidirectional TVS diode,
we would essentially have

the same type of
characteristic in reverse.
Now, there is a second type of diode
called a snapback diode,

and a snapback TVS diode
basically has a transfer function
that looks something like this
where it snaps in this direction
and then comes back to zero.
And similarly in the other direction,
basically has a snap like this

and then continues down into
the negative current direction.
Now these two types of TVS diodes

can be used for RF line
protection if the wave amplitude

sits within a certain
range of applied voltages.
And that range is known as VWRM
or the Working Reverse Voltage.

And that is basically
this range of voltages
from here to here.
So this is the range of applied voltages

where the TVS diode
basically doesn't conduct
and looks like a perfect insulator.

Now, there is a little bit of
leakage current, of course,

this curve does not ever
go perfectly to zero

except when the applied
voltage is exactly zero,
but, you get the idea there's gonna be

such low leakage current
as to be negligible
in most applications.
So this VWRM value, needs to be larger
than the voltage amplitude of this wave
traveling along the transmission line.

So we're gonna call that
requirement number two right here.

This is our second
requirement that we want
for a TVS diode on an RF line.

Next, if you know
anything about TVS diodes,
then you should know that all TVS diodes
have a small amount of capacitance,

and that capacitance exists
across the two terminals
on the TVS diode.

So that capacitance
needs to be very small.

Now, there's a very
simple way to understand
why this capacitance needs to be small.
There's really two ways.

The first thing you can
do is you can compare

this capacitance with the
expected capacitance of this line

in the region where
the signal is occupied.
And so if this capacitance is very small,
then most of the return current
is going to pass into the ground plane

through capacitive coupling
from the line to ground.
And that's exactly what defines
the characteristic impedance of this line.
So if this capacitance is very small,
that creates very small deviation

in the characteristic
impedance of this line
as the wave travels.

So we don't wanna create
an impedance deviation
by placing this TVS diode along the line.
The other way you can think about this

is you can think about the
impedance of this path to ground,

and we would like for the
impedance for this path to ground
to be very high.
And of course, that's going to demand

a very small capacitance
on this TVS diode.
So that's requirement number three.
Next, what is the fourth requirement
for a good TVS diode on an RF line?
Well, the requirement here

for a TVS diode on an RF line
relates to the capacitance,

but what we would like to
see is we would like to have

a very small change in
capacitance with applied voltage.
Now the capacitance of this TVS diode

across the terminals
can change with voltage,

We don't want to have a sudden
increase in the capacitance

when we get to the high or
low points along this wave,
that's going to ensure that we always have

a high impedance path
between this line and ground.
So these curves showing
the capacitance versus applied voltage
typically look something like this.
If I were to just draw out a graph

they basically look something like this.

They have a logarithmic
shape but flipped over.

So we wanna make sure that
change is reasonably small.
Typical values for the capacitance
that you might find in a TVS diode,

can be anywhere from
picofarads down to femtofarads
so they can be pretty small values.

And the higher up in the
frequency range you go,
of course, you want to ensure
that you have lower and lower capacitance.

You also wanna make sure that
this capacitance is stable.
